blocks.text: The word translated “profit” asks what lasting surplus or advantage people can secure from all their labor “under the sun.” This question in verse 3 frames the chapter’s observations about recurring natural cycles, human weariness, and the limits of wisdom: the concern is not simply whether work has value, but whether it leaves an enduring gain.

The speaker is called Qohelet, rendered here as “the Preacher.” The book presents this speaker in a royal persona—“son of David” and king in Jerusalem—yet never actually names Solomon. Its repeated word translated “vanity” is hebel, the concrete image of vapor or breath. Rather than requiring one fixed meaning, the term can evoke transience, frustration, insubstantiality, enigma, or an absurd mismatch; that range helps explain the force of the opening refrain and the later description of wisdom as “a striving after wind.”

The received book distinguishes an opening third-person frame from Qohelet’s extended first-person speech, while its closing epilogue returns to a third-person voice and evaluates Qohelet. Ecclesiastes is preserved in the Masoretic Hebrew text, fragmentary Hebrew manuscripts from Qumran, and an exceptionally literal Greek version. Its late Hebrew features and loanwords lead many critical scholars to date it to the Persian or early Hellenistic period, while a Hebrew manuscript shows that the book circulated by about 175–150 BCE.
